title: Adaptation
full_review:
"Adaptation" (Columbia) is the oddball movie of the year, about a blocked screenwriter who out of desperation writes himself and his frustrations into his film adaptation.

It's the kind of out-there movie that some will find brilliant while others will scratch their heads or look longingly toward the exit door.

The movie is about real-life screenwriter Charlie Kaufman ("Being John Malkovich"), who is played by Nicolas Cage. Cage also plays Charlie's fictional twin brother, Donald, who is writing a first screenplay whose cheesy plot has already attracted studio interest, much to his serious brother's chagrin.

Charlie can't get a handle on adapting the nonfiction book "The Orchid Thief" by Susan Orlean (Meryl Streep), a reporter who tracked down fanatical orchid breeder John Laroche (Chris Cooper) in the Florida Everglades and wrote about his colorful past and how his passion inspired her to find some passion in her own life.

We see how she pursued her story about Laroche -- and Cooper is terrific as the seedy yet occasionally profound eccentric, while Streep's journalist is less believable when she undergoes a bizarre personality transformation in the contrived finale.

After feeling he must write about the beauty of the orchid -- a theme he knows won't sell with the studio suits -- Charlie decides instead to write himself and his quest into the film.

His scornful advice to his brother to not stoop to hack-level writing about a serial killer with a multiple personality falls on sweetly deaf ears and soon easygoing Donald sells his script and is considered Hollywood's new hot writer. This sibling relationship is what makes the movie touching; Charlie is jealous and acid-tongued, but Donald just keeps on loving and trying to help his brother no matter how mean-spirited Charlie becomes.

Although Charlie keeps assuring his agent his writing is going well, he is consumed with self-loathing, seeing himself as fat, bald and ugly and unable to get at all physical with the woman (Cara Seymour) who likes him.

Neurotically shy, he flies to New York to meet the book's author, then can't get up the courage to say hello even when she happens to share an elevator with him. When his brother meets Susan it sets off a chain of violent events that plunge the film toward a crazed conclusion that goes quite over the top. This is where the script's basis in fact meets fiction, and the transition is a jarring one.

Written by Charlie Kaufman and directed by Spike Jonze, the film is highly original and engrossing in its depiction of Charlie as a creative person striving to excel in an industry that only cares about the box-office take, as evidenced by Donald's instant success with a cliched script. But Charlie's whiny character gradually grates on the nerves, his constant insecurities and pathetic self-lacerations making him less sympathetic even as we feel for his desire to do a good job.

Taken in its comic-satiric context, the movie's deadly conclusion springs from a fevered imagination to give some kind of an ending to an impossible-to-adapt film. It certainly shouldn't be taken as an endorsement of Susan and John's behavior. The wildly melodramatic ending may be deliberate but it's so at odds with the rest of the film's dogged but nutty earnestness it simply doesn't work.

Due to brief but intense violence, recreational drug use, a sexual encounter, implied masturbation, fleeting nudity and glimpses of a pornographic Web site, much rough language and some profanity, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-IV -- adults, with reservations. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
